source.title: The Central Bank Question
source.summary: What central banks actually do, why every country has one, and the fundamental tension with Islamic economics.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Central banks solved real problems: bank runs, credit crunches, currency instability. But they also created new ones: moral hazard, inflation bias, regressive distributional effects. This episode gives central banking an even-handed examination: what it does well, where it fails, and what the bayt al-mal as an Islamic monetary authority might look like. Turkey's inflation crisis illustrates what happens when central bank independence is compromised. The fundamental tension: Islamic economics prohibits interest rates, but modern central banking runs entirely on them. Can that circle be squared?

linkedin.post: Every country has a central bank for the same reason every ancient civilization had a treasury: financial chaos destroys societies. Central banks solved real problems—bank runs, credit crunches, currency instability. But they created new ones: moral hazard, inflation bias, regressive effects on wealth distribution. The fundamental tension with Islamic economics is stark. Modern central banking runs entirely on interest rate manipulation. Islamic monetary theory prohibits this core mechanism. Turkey's recent inflation crisis illustrates what happens when central bank independence is compromised. Political pressure led to rate cuts during inflation spikes. The result: inflation hit 85%. Could the bayt al-mal function as an Islamic monetary authority? What tools would replace interest rate policy? These aren't just theoretical questions—they're essential for any serious Islamic economic system. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-mm-2

short_video.hook: Every country has a central bank for the same reason ancient civilizations had treasuries.
short_video.voiceover: Central banks exist to prevent financial chaos. Bank runs and credit crunches can destroy economies faster than wars. They solved these problems but created new ones: moral hazard, inflation bias. Here's the tension with Islamic economics: central banking runs entirely on interest rate manipulation—the mechanism Islamic finance prohibits. Turkey's recent crisis proves this matters. When political pressure compromised central bank independence, inflation hit eighty-five percent. Could the bayt al-mal work as an Islamic monetary authority? That's the billion-dollar question for genuine Islamic economic systems.
